rewrites.prompt: A Tsumeb engineering firm needs N$300 000 to pay wages and buy steel for a large order that its customer will pay for in 60 days, and N$250 000 for a lathe it will use for eight years. Explain the difference between its short-term and long-term needs for finance.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A short-term need is expected to be settled within about a year and comes from day-to-day trading; a long-term need lasts more than about a year and comes from spending on assets that will earn revenue over several years. The N$300 000 for wages and steel is a short-term need: the customer pays in 60 days and the money returns. The N$250 000 lathe is a long-term need: it earns its cost back over eight years. The boundary is how long the money stays tied up, not the size of the sum - here the larger amount is the short-term one.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - how long the money is committed before trading returns it.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the firm - the N$300 000 returned in 60 days against the N$250 000 lathe used for eight years; 1 mark if applied without the timing.
Boundary: length of time, not the size of the amount - an answer that uses the size has missed it.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek furniture maker made a profit of N$40 000 in March but ended the month with N$15 000 less in the bank, because a hotel that ordered N$120 000 of furniture will pay in May. Explain the difference between the cash it holds and the profit it has made.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Cash is the money the business actually holds and can pay with today; profit is revenue minus the costs of earning it over a period, recorded when the sale is made rather than when money moves. The furniture maker's N$40 000 profit counts the hotel's N$120 000 order as March revenue, but the hotel's money arrives in May, while the timber and wages for that order were paid in March. So the business added value in March yet ended the month with less cash, which is why it has to watch both figures.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - money held now against revenue minus costs recorded when the sale is made.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the furniture maker - a March profit that includes the hotel order, with cash falling because payment comes in May; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: basis of measurement and timing; the two figures answer different questions.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: Two Namibian companies are being wound up: one after a supplier it owes N$2 million applied to the court, the other because its owners are retiring and closing a business that can pay all its debts. Explain the difference between compulsory and voluntary liquidation, using these two companies.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Compulsory liquidation is forced on a company from outside, typically after an unpaid creditor applies to a court; voluntary liquidation is begun by the company itself, through its shareholders. The first company is in compulsory liquidation: its supplier, owed N$2 million, applied to the court, so the company chose neither the moment nor the outcome. The second is in voluntary liquidation: its owners are closing a business that can pay its debts, tidily, on retirement. So a voluntary winding up does not by itself mean the company could not pay what it owed.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - who starts the process, and whether it implies insolvency.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the two companies - the supplier's court application against the retiring owners' decision; 1 mark if only one is applied.
Boundary: an outside application against a decision of the shareholders.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek bus company in financial difficulty has been placed in administration, while a failed clothing retailer has gone into liquidation. Explain the difference between administration and liquidation for these two companies.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Both are formal procedures that hand control of a struggling company to an appointed outsider, but they differ in purpose. Administration is an attempt to rescue: the administrator runs the bus company, normally protected from creditors enforcing their claims, and tries to keep it operating or to sell it as a working business, so it may come out still trading. Liquidation is the end of the company: the retailer's liquidator sells its assets, pays creditors in the legal order and passes anything left to shareholders, and the company ceases to exist. Administration that fails is commonly followed by liquidation.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - rescue against closure; temporary against terminal.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the bus company and the retailer; 1 mark if only one is applied.
Boundary: purpose and outcome, not procedure alone; the two can occur in sequence.

rewrites.prompt: A Rehoboth delivery business buys a van, insures it for a year, replaces a worn tyre and fits a refrigeration unit. Explain the difference between capital and revenue expenditure, using these four payments.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets kept and used for more than a year; revenue expenditure is spending on running the business day to day, used up within the period. Buying the van and fitting the refrigeration unit are capital expenditure: both give the business capabilities it will use for years. The year's insurance and the replacement tyre are revenue expenditure: they keep the van doing what it already did and are used up within the period. The boundary is what is bought and how long it is used, not how much it costs.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - length of use: assets kept beyond a year against spending used up in the period.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the four payments, including the repair-against-improvement boundary; 1 mark if only some are classified correctly.
Boundary: length of use, not size of amount.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Keetmanshoop mechanic needs N$150 000 for equipment. She could use her savings or borrow from a bank. Explain the difference between owner's investment and a bank loan as ways of raising this N$150 000.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Owner's investment comes from the owner's own wealth, carries no interest and has no repayment schedule; a bank loan comes from outside, carries interest and must be repaid whether or not the business trades well. If the mechanic uses her savings, she risks her own money but has no monthly repayments on the N$150 000 while the workshop builds up trade. A bank loan would leave her savings untouched, but she would owe interest and scheduled repayments from the first month, and the bank would usually want security, such as the equipment itself.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - own wealth without interest or repayment against outside money repaid with interest.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the mechanic's N$150 000 - her savings at risk against repayments and security; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: both sides of the difference, with a consequence stated.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek printing company owns an empty warehouse in Brakwater and the building it prints in. Explain the difference between selling unwanted assets and sale and leaseback for this company.
rewrites.canonical_answer: In a sale of unwanted assets the business disposes of something it no longer uses and keeps the cash; in sale and leaseback it sells an asset it still uses and then pays to carry on using it. Selling the empty Brakwater warehouse is a sale of an unwanted asset: the company gains cash and gives up nothing it needs. Selling the building it prints in and leasing it back also raises cash, but the company then takes on a continuing lease cost and loses the building's future value, in exchange for staying where it is.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - an asset no longer used against one still used and leased back.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the warehouse and the print building, with the continuing lease cost as the consequence; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: both sides of the difference, with a consequence stated.

rewrites.prompt: A Swakopmund wholesaler wants N$80 000 to refit its showroom and plans to raise it by cutting its inventory and chasing customers who pay late. Explain the difference between using working capital as a source of finance and managing working capital, for this wholesaler.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Using working capital as a source means deliberately releasing cash from the operating cycle to fund something specific; managing it means keeping the cycle balanced so the business can pay its debts as they fall due. The wholesaler's plan uses working capital as a source: cutting inventory and collecting from late payers releases the N$80 000 for the refit. Managing working capital is the continuing job alongside it: if inventory is cut too far the wholesaler may run out of stock and lose sales, and if customers are pressed too hard some may buy elsewhere.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a one-off financing decision against an ongoing operating one.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the wholesaler - releasing N$80 000 from inventory and receivables, against the balance it must still keep; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: both sides of the difference, with a consequence stated.

rewrites.prompt: A Namibian mining company listed on the stock exchange needs N$500 million for a new shaft. Explain the difference between raising this money through share capital and through a debenture.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Share capital is equity: buyers become part-owners, the money is not repaid and no interest is paid, though dividends are expected. A debenture is borrowing: holders are lenders, not owners, interest is paid at a fixed rate whether or not the company makes a profit, and the sum must be repaid on the redemption date. For the mining company, new shares would dilute existing shareholders' control but place no fixed burden on its cash flow if metal prices fall. A debenture would leave control untouched, but the interest would have to be paid in a bad year for metal prices as well as a good one.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - ownership against lending.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the mining company - dilution without a fixed cash burden, against unchanged control with interest due every year; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: ownership versus lending, with the consequence stated.

rewrites.prompt: A Namibian telecoms company could borrow N$300 million by issuing debentures or by taking a loan from one bank. Explain the difference between a debenture and a bank loan for this company.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A debenture is a loan certificate a company issues to many holders, at a fixed interest rate with a fixed redemption date; a bank loan is borrowed from a single lender on terms agreed with that lender and repaid in instalments. If the telecoms company issues debentures, its cost and repayment date are fixed in advance and cannot be renegotiated at will, because many investors hold them on published terms. A bank loan's schedule, security and conditions are settled with one lender, so if trading changes the company can go back to the bank and ask to revise them.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - many holders on fixed published terms against one lender on negotiated terms.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the telecoms company's N$300 million - fixed terms against terms it can revisit; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the source of the borrowing and its terms, with the consequence stated.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A two-partner accounting practice in Oshakati needs N$200 000 to open a second office. Explain the difference between admitting a new partner and taking a bank loan to raise this money.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A new partner supplies capital that carries no interest and no obligation to repay, but takes a permanent share of profit and of control. A bank loan leaves ownership untouched but must be repaid with interest whatever the practice earns. If the practice admits a third partner, the N$200 000 costs nothing in repayments, but the two existing partners share future profits three ways and must agree decisions with the newcomer. A loan keeps the practice in their hands, but it commits them to repayments even if the second office is slow to find clients.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a permanent share of profit and control against repayment with interest.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the practice's second office; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: both sides of the difference, with a consequence stated.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek bakery that owns its premises needs N$600 000 for new ovens. Explain the difference between a mortgage on its premises and an unsecured bank loan as ways of raising this money.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A mortgage is secured on property: the business names an asset the lender can look to if repayments are not met; an unsecured loan names no such asset. Because the bakery owns its premises, a mortgage on them could provide the N$600 000 over many years at a lower rate, since the lender has the building as protection - but the bakery could lose its premises if it cannot keep up the repayments. An unsecured loan puts no property at risk, but with less protection the lender generally lends less, for less time, at a higher rate. How a lender recovers a property, and how quickly, depends on national law.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether a named asset backs the loan.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the bakery's N$600 000 - size, term and rate against the risk to its premises; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: security, with the consequence for size, term and rate; any statement about enforcement qualified as depending on national law.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Walvis Bay sole trader running a fish shop and a Namibian fishing group listed as a public limited company both want to expand. Explain the difference between the sources of finance available to the sole trader and to the public limited company.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A sole trader cannot issue shares, because an unincorporated business has none, so the fish shop's capital comes from the owner's own resources, retained profit, borrowing, trade credit and asset finance. A public limited company may offer its shares for sale to the general public, so the fishing group can raise equity on a scale the sole trader cannot. That legal difference is the decisive one. What follows from it is a tendency rather than a rule: the company borrows as a separate legal person on its own assets and record, but limited liability protects its owners, not its lenders, so a lender may still want security.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the sale of shares to the public, which a sole trader cannot make.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the fish shop and the fishing group, with the consequence for how each can raise money; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the decisive legal difference; do not reward limited liability as reducing the lender's risk, and keep anything about lender willingness conditional.
